The core sense involves a cry that comes from the depths of desperation, seeking rescue. The Quran describes how those facing punishment will 'yajʾarūna' — cry out in supplication — but their plea will come too late.

meaning.en: The root jīm-dhāl-ʿayn (ج-ذ-ع) fundamentally denotes the trunk of a tree, particularly a palm trunk, and that which is raw or fresh. It conveys the sturdy central stem of a tree after the branches are removed, and by extension, something in a raw, unprocessed state. The core sense involves the central, supporting axis of a plant. The Quran tells Maryam during childbirth: 'wa huzzī ilayki bi jidhʿi al-nakhlati' — and shake toward you the trunk of the palm tree — providing her with sustenance at the moment of greatest vulnerability.

meaning.en: The root hāʾ-zāy-mīm (ه-ز-م) fundamentally denotes defeat, routing, and putting to flight. It conveys the act of overcoming an enemy decisively, breaking their ranks and scattering them. The core sense involves decisive victory that shatters opposition. The Quran uses this root for the defeat of the disbelievers at the Battle of Badr: 'sayuhzamu al-jamʿu wa yuwallūna al-dubur' — the assembly will be defeated and they will turn their backs in flight — a prophesied divine victory.
meaning.ar: قال ابن فارس: الهاء والزاء والميم أصل واحد يدل على كسر الشيء ورده، ومنه هزمت الجيش أهزمه هزماً، إذا كسرته ورددته. والهزيمة: الكسرة في الحرب.

meaning.en: The root hāʾ-mīm-zāy (ه-م-ز) fundamentally denotes prodding, goading, and slandering. It conveys two interconnected ideas: (1) the physical act of prodding an animal with a stick to urge it forward; (2) the verbal act of backbiting, slandering, and making derogatory insinuations. The core sense involves sharp, piercing provocation. The Quran condemns 'humaza' — the habitual slanderer who wounds others with his tongue.
meaning.ar: «الْهَمْزُ: دَفْعٌ وَضَرْبٌ. يُقَالُ: هَمَزَهُ يَهْمِزُهُ هَمْزًا: دَفَعَهُ وَضَرَبَهُ. وَالْهَمْزُ: الْغِيبَةُ وَالطَّعْنُ فِي الْأَعْرَاضِ.»

It conveys the posture of someone rushing eagerly or fearfully, with neck extended and eyes fixed on what lies ahead. The core sense involves forward-focused urgency. The Quran uses this root for the disbelievers rushing toward the caller on the Day of Judgment — 'muhṭiʿīna ilā al-dāʿī' — hastening with outstretched necks, unable to look away.

It conveys the act of intertwining fibers to create a rope or cord — the careful, deliberate twisting of strands into a unified, strong whole. The core sense involves tension through torsion. The Quran uses this root in the story of the woman who unraveled her spun thread after it was tightly twisted — a metaphor for those who break their oaths after confirming them.

meaning.en: The root fāʾ-zāy-zāy (ف-ز-ز) fundamentally denotes being startled, terrified, and fleeing in panic. It conveys the sudden, intense fear that causes one to jump or flee — the instinctive reaction to an unexpected threat. The core sense involves a violent disruption of composure. The Quran uses this root for the terror that will strike on the Day of Judgment, when the most composed will be 'mafzūʿīn' — seized with terror.
meaning.ar: الْفَاءُ وَالزَّاءُ وَالزَّاءُ الْمُكَرَّرَةُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الْقَلَقِ وَالِاضْطِرَابِ. وَمِنْهُ قَوْلُهُمْ: رَجُلٌ فَزٌّ، أَيْ: قَلِقٌ لَا يَثْبُتُ فِي مَكَانٍ.

meaning.en: The root fāʾ-rāʾ-ṭāʾ (ف-ر-ط) fundamentally denotes excess, transgression, and that which is sent before or neglected. It conveys two distinct yet related ideas: (1) going beyond proper bounds, whether in extravagance or negligence; (2) that which is sent ahead or done in advance, whether good deeds or bad. The core sense involves exceeding limits — either surpassing them or falling short. The Quran uses 'furāṭ' for a punishment that is doubled and 'tafarrāṭū' for negligence toward divine commands.
meaning.ar: الْفَاءُ وَالرَّاءُ وَالتَّاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى طِيبِ الْمَاءِ وَعُذُوبَتِهِ، يُقَالُ مَاءٌ فُرَاتٌ أَيْ عَذْبٌ.

meaning.en: The root fāʾ-sīn-ḥāʾ (ف-س-ح) fundamentally denotes spaciousness, expansion, and making room. It conveys the act of creating space where there was crowding, widening a confined area to accommodate more. The core sense involves gracious accommodation and generous expansion. The Quran commands: 'idhā qīla lakum tafassaḥū fī al-majālisi fafsaḥū yafsaḥi Allāhu lakum' — when you are told to make room in assemblies, make room, and Allah will make room for you — linking social courtesy to divine reward.
meaning.ar: الْفَاءُ وَالسِّينُ وَالْحَاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى السَّعَةِ وَالِانْبِسَاطِ، يُقَالُ: مَكَانٌ فَسِيحٌ أَيْ وَاسِعٌ، وَفَسَحَ لَهُ فِي الْمَجْلِسِ أَيْ وَسَّعَ لَهُ.

meaning.en: The root fāʾ-qāf-dāl (ف-ق-د) fundamentally denotes losing, missing, and being unable to find. It conveys the painful experience of discovering that something or someone is absent, lost, or gone — the cognitive and emotional recognition of absence. The core sense involves lack discovered. The Quran recounts Jacob's grief: 'yā asafā ʿalā Yūsuf' — Oh, my sorrow for Joseph — after 'faqada' (missing) his beloved son. It also speaks of those who 'tafqidūnī' — you will find me missing.

meaning.en: The root fāʾ-jīm-jīm (ف-ج-ج) fundamentally denotes a wide path, a broad mountain pass, and a cleft. It conveys the idea of a spacious opening or passageway, whether a natural gap between mountains or a broad road that is easy to traverse. The core sense involves expansiveness and openness. The Quran uses 'fijājan' for the spacious paths that Allah created through the mountains — signs of His provision for human travel and exploration.
meaning.ar: الْفَاءُ وَالْجِيمُ وَالْجِيمُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى انْفِرَاجِ الشَّيْءِ وَاتِّسَاعِهِ. يُقَالُ: فَجَّ الشَّيْءَ يَفُجُّهُ فَجًّا إِذَا فَتَحَهُ وَوَسَّعَهُ.

meaning.en: The root bāʾ-rāʾ-ḥāʾ (ب-ر-ح) fundamentally denotes departing, leaving, and being undeniable. It conveys two interconnected ideas: (1) the act of going away from a place, moving on; (2) that which is clearly, undeniably the case — that which 'does not leave' doubt. The core sense involves movement away from a fixed position. The Quran uses 'bāriḥ' for that which departs and the expression 'bariḥa' in the negative to indicate continuity.
meaning.ar: الْبَاءُ وَالرَّاءُ وَالْحَاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الْقَطْعِ وَالْفِرَاقِ. يُقَالُ بَرِحَ يَبْرَحُ بَرَاحًا إِذَا ذَهَبَ وَفَارَقَ.

It conveys the quality of something that is visually pleasing, radiant, and cause for joy — whether a beautiful garden, a splendid view, or a delightful experience. The core sense involves aesthetic joy. The Quran describes the earth after rain: 'fa ihtazzat wa rabat wa anbatat min kulli zawjin bahīj' — it stirs and swells and puts forth every lovely kind — the beauty of creation as a sign of the Creator.

meaning.en: The root bāʾ-hāʾ-mīm (ب-ه-م) fundamentally denotes obscurity, ambiguity, and the mute animals. It conveys two distinct ideas: (1) that which is unclear, obscure, or difficult to comprehend; (2) the category of livestock or beasts that do not speak — the 'bahīma', particularly the four-legged grazing animal. The core sense involves inarticulateness and lack of clarity. The root encompasses both the voiceless creatures and the voiceless concepts that resist easy understanding.
meaning.ar: الْبَاءُ وَالْهَاءُ وَالْمِيمُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى إِبْهَامٍ وَتَغْطِيَةٍ. يُقَالُ: بَهَمَ الْأَمْرُ إِذَا أَشْكَلَ وَالْتَبَسَ.

The Quran uses 'ṭafiqa' to describe David and Solomon's immediate engagement in righting a wrong or examining a matter — a verb that captures both the start and the persistent continuation of an action.

meaning.en: The root bāʾ-dhāl-rāʾ (ب-ذ-ر) fundamentally denotes scattering, sowing seeds, and squandering. It conveys the act of dispersing seeds in the earth for cultivation and, by extension, the wasteful dissipation of resources. The core sense involves dispersal — whether purposeful (sowing) or reckless (squandering). The Quran uses 'tabdhīr' for wasteful spending, linking it to kinship with Satan: 'inna al-mubadhdhirīna kānū ikhwāna al-shayāṭīn' — indeed the wasteful are brothers of the devils.
meaning.ar: الْبَاءُ وَالذَّالُ وَالرَّاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى تَفْرِيقِ الشَّيْءِ وَإِضَاعَتِهِ. يُقَالُ: بَذَرَ الشَّيْءَ يَبْذُرُهُ بَذْرًا، إِذَا فَرَّقَهُ وَأَضَاعَهُ.

meaning.en: The root ẓāʾ-mīm-hamza (ظ-م-أ) fundamentally denotes thirst, intense desire for water, and longing. It conveys the physical sensation of needing water and, metaphorically, the soul's deep yearning for what it lacks. The core sense involves acute need and craving. The Quran uses 'ẓamaʾ' in the context of the righteous who will not suffer thirst in Paradise — their every need satisfied by divine generosity.
meaning.ar: قال ابن فارس: (ظ م أ) الظاء والميم والهمزة أصلٌ واحد يدل على خلاف الرِّيِّ، وهو الظَّمَأُ، وهو العطش. ويقال: ظَمِئَ يَظْمَأُ ظَمَأً، فهو ظَمْآنُ، والمرأة ظَمْأَى.

meaning.en: The root ṭāʾ-fāʾ-hamza (ط-ف-أ) fundamentally denotes extinguishing, putting out, and quenching fire. It conveys the act of ending a flame or fire, stopping its burning and light. The core sense involves the termination of heat and light. The Quran uses this root in the powerful metaphor: 'yurīdūna an yuṭfiʾū nūra Allāhi bi afwāhihim' — they wish to extinguish the light of Allah with their mouths — but Allah completes His light despite the disbelievers.

meaning.en: The root ḍād-ghayn-thāʾ (ض-غ-ث) fundamentally denotes a handful of mixed herbs, a confused bundle, and a confused dream. It conveys the act of laying a foundation — the starting point of construction, whether of a physical building, an institution, or an argument. meaning.en: The root dhāl-hamza-bāʾ (ذ-أ-ب) fundamentally denotes the wolf, the predatory canine of the wilderness. It conveys the specific animal known for its cunning, predatory nature, and menace to livestock. The core sense involves a threat that operates through stealth and strength — a predator that evokes primal fear. The Quran recounts the brothers of Joseph using the wolf as their alibi: 'wa akhāfu an yaʾkulahu al-dhiʾb' — I fear that a wolf may eat him — a lie that masked their own betrayal.
meaning.ar: الذَّاءُ وَالْبَاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الْأَخْذِ وَالِانْتِهَابِ، وَمِنْهُ الذِّئْبُ لِأَنَّهُ يَذْهَبُ بِالشَّيْءِ وَيَأْخُذُهُ.

The core sense involves capacity utilized to its limit. The Quran uses this root for Noah's ark: 'iḥmil fīhā min kullin zawjayni ithnayn' — load into it of every kind a pair — and for hearts filled with hatred.
meaning.ar: قال ابن فارس في مقاييس اللغة: 'الشين والحاء والنون أصل واحد يدل على ملء الشيء حتى يضيق. يقال: شحنت السفينة، أي ملأتها. والمشحون: المملوء.'

meaning.en: The root shīn-hamza-mīm (ش-أ-م) fundamentally denotes ill omen, the left side, and misfortune. It conveys the concept of bad luck, unluckiness, and the direction of the left as being associated with inauspiciousness. The core sense involves what is foreboding and unlucky — the opposite of 'yumn' (blessing, right side). The Quran mentions 'al-mashʾama' — the people of the left hand — those who will receive their book in their left hand on Judgment Day.
meaning.ar: الشِّينُ وَالْهَمْزَةُ وَالْمِيمُ أَصْلَانِ: أَحَدُهُمَا يَدُلُّ عَلَى ضِدِّ الْيُمْنِ، وَالْآخَرُ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الْعَلَامَةِ. فَالْأَوَّلُ: الشُّؤْمُ، وَهُوَ ضِدُّ الْيُمْنِ.

meaning.en: The root wāw-ṣād-dāl (و-ص-د) fundamentally denotes being firm, established, and the closure of a door or gate. It conveys the idea of something being made firm and shut tight — a door that is bolted, locked, and cannot be opened. The core sense involves impenetrable closure. The Quran uses this root for the gates of Hell that are 'muʾṣada' — firmly shut upon its inhabitants, with no possibility of escape.
meaning.ar: الْوَاوُ وَالصَّادُ وَالدَّالُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الْإِطْبَاقِ وَالْإِغْلَاقِ. يُقَالُ: أَوْصَدْتُ الْبَابَ إِذَا أَغْلَقْتُهُ، وَآصَدْتُهُ مِثْلُهُ. وَالْأُصْدَةُ: الْعَتَبَةُ.

meaning.en: The root hamza-ṣād-rāʾ (أ-ص-ر) fundamentally denotes binding, pressing, and a heavy burden or covenant. meaning.en: The root dhāl-rāʾ-wāw (ذ-ر-و) fundamentally denotes scattering, winnowing, and dispersing. It conveys the act of spreading something by the force of wind — the farmer winnowing grain, the wind dispersing dust, or action being scattered to naught. The Quran declares: 'wa qadimnā ilā mā ʿamilū min ʿamalin fajaʿalnāhu habāʾan manthūrā' — and We will approach what they have done of deeds and make them as scattered dust — utterly void of substance.

meaning.en: The root shīn-nūn-hamza (ش-ن-أ) fundamentally denotes hatred, enmity, and intense aversion. It conveys a deep-seated, bitter hatred that wells up in the heart against someone. The core sense involves visceral animosity. The Quran warns: 'wa lā yajrimannakum shanaʾānu qawmin ʿalā allā taʿdilū' — and let not the hatred of a people incite you to not be just — a profound ethical command to uphold justice even against those you hate.

meaning.en: The root hamza-bāʾ-lām (أ-ب-ل) fundamentally denotes camels, particularly the herd of camels, and that which is well-prepared or organized. It conveys the specific grouping of camels as livestock and, by extension, the skill and organization required to manage them. The core sense involves the valuable herd animal of desert life. The Quran asks mankind to contemplate the creation of camels: 'a falā yanẓurūna ilā al-ibili kayfa khuliqat' — do they not look at the camels, how they are created?

meaning.en: The root hamza-fāʾ-fāʾ (أ-ف-ف) fundamentally denotes the expression of annoyance, disgust, and irritation. It conveys the sound 'uff' — the smallest word of complaint or disrespect. The core sense involves the minimal vocalization of displeasure. The Quran commands: 'fa lā taqul lahumā uffin wa lā tanharhumā' — do not say to them [parents] 'uff' and do not repel them — forbidding even the slightest expression of irritation toward parents, elevating their status to the highest degree.

meaning.en: The root ṣād-bāʾ-wāw (ص-ب-و) fundamentally denotes inclination, longing, and the condition of youth. It conveys the natural tendency of the young toward desire, the passionate inclination of the heart toward something, and the early morning wind that brings news. The core sense involves a strong, directional pull — the heart being drawn toward what it loves. The word 'ṣabwatan' refers to youthful passion and the tender inclinations of early life.

It conveys the act of shoving someone away with force and contempt — the physical manifestation of rejection and disdain. The core sense involves violent repulsion. meaning.en: The root jīm-dāl-thāʾ (ج-د-ث) fundamentally denotes a grave, tomb, and burial place. It conveys the specific physical location where the dead are interred — the cavity in the earth that houses the deceased until the Resurrection. The core sense involves the final earthly resting place of the body. The Quran describes the Day of Judgment: 'wa idhā al-qubūru buʿthirat' — and when the graves are scattered — when the dead emerge from their 'jadath' for judgment.

meaning.en: The root jīm-zāy-hamza (ج-ز-أ) fundamentally denotes a portion, part, recompense, and sufficiency. It conveys the concept of dividing something into parts, each being a distinct share, and by extension, the reward or recompense that is a fitting portion for one's deeds. The core sense involves equitable apportionment. The word 'jazāʾ' — recompense — is central to Quranic theology: every soul receives what it has earned, whether reward or punishment, in perfect justice.

meaning.en: The root kāf-bāʾ-tāʾ (ك-ب-ت) fundamentally denotes suppressing, repressing, and throwing down in humiliation. It conveys the act of subduing something forcefully, casting it down so that it cannot rise, and the internal suppression of anger or malice. The core sense involves forceful suppression and humiliation. The Quran uses this root for the defeat and humiliation of the disbelievers: 'li yaqṭaʿa ṭarafan mina alladhīna kafarū aw yakbatahum' — to cut off a part of those who disbelieve or to suppress them.

meaning.en: The root lām-hāʾ-bāʾ (ل-ه-ب) fundamentally denotes a flame, blaze, and the flickering of fire. It conveys the visible, dancing tongue of fire that rises from burning material — the bright, hot, and dangerous corona of combustion. The core sense involves the leaping flame itself, distinct from the ember or the fuel. Surat al-Masad famously mentions 'Abū Lahab' — the Father of Flame — whose very name became synonymous with his destined punishment.

It conveys the state of being fed up, losing interest, and finding something tedious after prolonged exposure. The core sense involves the exhaustion of enthusiasm through repetition. The Quran declares that the angels never tire of worship: 'wa hum lā yasʾamūn' — and they do not weary — in contrast to human nature, which easily grows tired of sustained devotion.

meaning.en: The triliteral root Ṣ-B-A (ص-ب-أ) refers to the Sabians (al-Ṣābi'ūn), a religious group mentioned in the Quran alongside believers, Jews, Christians, and Magians. The Sabians are traditionally identified as a monotheistic or semi-monotheistic community, possibly the Mandaeans of Mesopotamia or a related group. The root is exclusively used in the Quran to designate this religious community, and God promises that those among them who believe in Him and the Last Day and do righteousness shall have their reward.

meaning.en: The quadriliteral root Z-Q-M (ز-ق-م) specifically denotes the Zaqqum tree, a horrid tree that grows in the depths of Hellfire, mentioned in the Quran as the food of the sinful. Its fruit is described as being like the heads of devils, and it boils in the bellies like molten brass. The root is exclusively used in the Quran for this infernal tree, serving as a powerful symbol of divine punishment.

meaning.en: The root t-w-r (ت-و-ر) in Arabic conveys the core semantic field of 'a single occurrence, instance, or turn of events.' It denotes a specific point in time or a particular occasion, often implying repetition or alternation. The classical lexicographers, particularly Ibn Faris, identify its primary meaning as 'a time' (مرة) or 'a turn' (نوبة), with the underlying notion of something that comes around or recurs. This root is distinct from other time-related roots (e.g., ز-م-ن for 'time' as a continuum, ح-ي-ن for 'a period') in that it emphasizes the discrete, countable nature of an event or action

meaning.en: The quadriliteral root qāf-rāʼ-ṭāʼ-sīn (ق-ر-ط-س) is a loanword of Greek origin (χάρτης, chartēs, meaning papyrus or sheet of writing material), referring to qirṭās (قِرْطَاس) — a sheet of parchment, papyrus, or paper used for writing. The term entered Arabic through Aramaic intermediaries and reflects the ancient Near Eastern scribal culture of sacred and official documents. In Quran 6:91, the polytheists challenge the Prophet with a polemical demand: they say God has not revealed anything to any human, and ask sarcastically about the Torah: "You make it into parchments (قَرَاطِيسَ) — you disclose some and conceal much." The broken plural qarāṭīs here refers to the Torah scrolls which the Jews were accused of fragmenting, revealing selectively, and hiding inconvenient passages — a polemical charge of scriptural manipulation that employs the materiality of the written medium to underscore the accusation.

meaning.en: The triliteral root ف-ر-ع (f-r-ʿ) encompasses the semantic field of branching, elevation, and distinction. Its primary meaning centers on the upper, elevated portions of a plant or tree—specifically the branches that extend upward. The root also carries connotations of prominence, superiority, and distinction. Extended meanings include that which is eminent, elevated, or outstanding, with the proper noun فرعون (Fir'awn/Pharaoh) deriving from this root, likely reflecting the ancient Egyptian royal title meaning 'great house' or 'lord of the elevated domain.' The root fundamentally denotes vertical extension and the uppermost part of anything.

meaning.en: The quadriliteral root shīn-rāʼ-thāʼ-mīm (ش-ر-ث-م) denotes a small, fragmented group or band of people. In classical Arabic lexicography, al-shirdhimah (الشِّرْذِمَة) refers to a remnant or a small detachment of a larger body, often carrying a connotation of insignificance or contempt. The root appears in Quran 26:54, where Pharaoh dismisses the fleeing Israelites as "indeed a small band" (لَشِرْذِمَةٌ), employing the term to belittle their numbers and justify his pursuit. Ibn Manzur in Lisān al-ʿArab notes that the term derives from the idea of being cut off or separated (القطعة من الشيء), emphasizing fragmentation from the whole.

meaning.en: The quadriliteral reduplicative root thāʼ-bāʼ-thāʼ-bāʼ (ث-ب-ث-ب) expresses the concept of wavering, vacillation, and being torn between two opposing states. The reduplication of the bivalent base th-b mirrors the semantic oscillation it denotes — the doubling of consonants phonetically enacts the back-and-forth movement of indecision. In Quran 4:143, the passive participle mudhabdhabīn (مُذَبْذَبِينَ) describes the hypocrites who waver between belief and disbelief, belonging neither to the believers nor the disbelievers. Al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī explains it as "being suspended between two matters, not settling on either one" (التردد بين أمرين لا يستقر على واحد منهما). The quadriliteral pattern faʿlala with radical repetition is a recognized Arabic morphological device for iterative or oscillating actions.

meaning.en: The quadriliteral root ʿayn-bāʼ-qāf-rāʼ (ع-ب-ق-ر) derives from the legendary toponym ʿAbqar (عَبْقَر), a mythical locale in pre-Islamic Arabian lore believed to be inhabited by jinn and renowned for producing wondrous, exquisite artifacts. From this association, the nisba adjective ʿabqariyy (عَبْقَرِيّ) came to denote anything of superlative quality, magnificence, and splendor — particularly rich, luxurious carpets and furnishings. Ibn Fāris in Maqāyīs al-Lugha remarks that the word originally referred to a place where marvelous things were crafted, and by extension came to describe anything extraordinary and beautiful.

meaning.en: The quadriliteral root ʿayn-rāʼ-jīm-nūn (ع-ر-ج-ن) refers to the ʿurjūn (عُرْجُون) — the dried, curved stalk of a date cluster after the fruit has been harvested. The root conveys the semantic core of curvature, bending, and arching, derived from the characteristic crescent-like shape of the desiccated date stalk. In Quran 36:39, God employs a precise astronomical simile: "And the moon — We have determined for it phases until it returns like the old date stalk" (كَالْعُرْجُونِ الْقَدِيمِ), comparing the waning crescent moon to the yellowed, curved ʿurjūn. Ibn Manẓūr notes that the ʿurjūn is specifically the stem of the date cluster (عرجون الكباسة) with its arched form, and the comparison to the old one (القديم) emphasizes its yellowish, withered quality mirroring the fading lunar crescent.

meaning.en: The quadriliteral reduplicative root ʿayn-sīn-ʿayn-sīn (ع-س-ع-س) encapsulates the dual motion of night — its advance and its retreat, its darkening and its passing. The reduplicative pattern (faʿlala with doubled radicals) is typical of Arabic verbs denoting temporal cycles or repeated natural phenomena, where the doubled consonants echo the rhythmic alternation of night and day. In Quran 81:17, God swears an oath "by the night when it departs" (وَاللَّيْلِ إِذَا عَسْعَسَ), using the verb ʿasʿasa which classical exegetes interpret as both "it approaches with its darkness" and "it recedes and departs." Al-Azharī in Tahdhīb al-Lugha notes that ʿasʿasa is among the rare Arabic words that can signify both the coming and the going of night (من الأضداد), making it a word of opposing meanings (aḍdād), encapsulating the full cycle of nocturnal darkness.

meaning.en: The quadriliteral reduplicative root ṣād-fāʼ-ṣād-fāʼ (ص-ف-ص-ف) denotes a vast, level, barren plain devoid of vegetation or topographic variation. meaning.en: The quadriliteral reduplicative root dāl-mīm-dāl-mīm (د-م-د-م) conveys the sense of overwhelming destruction, leveling, and complete annihilation through a repeated, crushing action. meaning.en: The quadriliteral root dāl-rāʼ-hāʼ-mīm (د-ر-ه-م) is a loanword of Greek origin (δραχμή, drachmē), referring to the dirham — a silver coin that served as the standard currency unit in the late antique Near East and early Islamic world. The term entered Arabic via Middle Persian (drahm) and Aramaic intermediaries, reflecting the deep commercial and cultural interconnections of pre-Islamic Arabia with the Byzantine and Sassanian empires. In Quran 12:20, Joseph's brothers sell him "for a paltry price — a few dirhams" (وَشَرَوْهُ بِثَمَنٍ بَخْسٍ دَرَاهِمَ مَعْدُودَةٍ), the adjective "counted few" emphasizing the meager, contemptible sum for which they bartered their brother. The word darāhim appears in its broken plural form, indicating a small, countable number of silver coins, and classical exegetes such as al-Ṭabarī note that the low price underscores the callousness of Joseph's brothers and the providential unfolding of his destiny.

meaning.en: The quadriliteral reduplicative root kāf-bāʼ-kāf-bāʼ (ك-ب-ك-ب) conveys the sense of overturning, upending, and casting headlong — particularly into perdition. In Quran 26:94, describing the fate of the idolaters and their false gods on the Day of Judgment, "they will be overturned into it [Hell]" (فَكُبْكِبُوا فِيهَا هُمْ وَالْغَاوُونَ), the verb kubkibū employs the reduplicative form to convey the forceful, mass casting of the condemned headlong into the Fire. meaning.en: The quadriliteral root qāf-shīn-ʿayn-rāʼ (ق-ش-ع-ر) expresses the physiological phenomenon of shivering, shuddering, and goosebumps — the involuntary contraction of skin in response to intense emotion, particularly fear or awe. In Quran 39:23, those who fear their Lord experience a physical reaction upon hearing the Quran: "their skins shiver" (تَقْشَعِرُّ مِنْهُ جُلُودُ الَّذِينَ يَخْشَوْنَ رَبَّهُمْ), followed by their skins and hearts softening to the remembrance of God. Al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī explains iqshaʿarra as "the skin contracting and standing up from fear" (تقبض الجلد وقيامه من الخوف), a word that captures the visceral, bodily dimension of spiritual awe (khashya).

meaning.en: The quadriliteral root qāf-ṭāʼ-mīm-rāʼ (ق-ط-م-ر) refers to the qiṭmīr (قِطْمِير) — the exceedingly thin, translucent membrane that envelops the pit inside a date fruit. This microscopic integument serves in the Quran as a powerful metaphor for insignificance, powerlessness, and the radical nothingness of what false deities possess. Classical exegetes note that the qiṭmīr is proverbially the most trivial and worthless thing imaginable in Arab culture — a filmy covering so insubstantial it is barely visible — making the verse a rhetorically devastating dismissal of polytheistic claims.

meaning.en: The quadriliteral root sīn-rāʼ-dāl-qāf (س-ر-د-ق) is a loanword of Middle Persian origin (srādag, meaning a tent, pavilion, or enclosure), referring to surādiq (سُرَادِق) — an encompassing wall, enclosure, or canopy, particularly the encircling pavilion of a royal tent. In Quran 18:29, the word describes the dreadful encirclement of Hellfire: "Indeed, We have prepared for the wrongdoers a Fire whose walls will surround them" (إِنَّا أَعْتَدْنَا لِلظَّالِمِينَ نَارًا أَحَاطَ بِهِمْ سُرَادِقُهَا). The surādiq of Hell is an enclosing wall or canopy of smoke and flame that completely surrounds the damned, leaving no avenue of escape — a terrifying inversion of the royal pavilion that usually connotes protection and honor. Al-Azharī notes that surādiq originally referred to the awning or curtain surrounding a tent (ما أحاط بالخباء), and its Quranic usage transforms this image of enclosure into one of inescapable punishment.

hadith.ar: عَنْ أَبِي هُرَيْرَةَ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «اشْتَكَتِ النَّارُ إِلَى رَبِّهَا فَقَالَتْ: يَا رَبِّ أَكَلَ بَعْضِي بَعْضًا فَأَذِنَ لَهَا بِنَفَسَيْنِ نَفَسٍ فِي الشِّتَاءِ وَنَفَسٍ فِي الصَّيْفِ»
hadith.en: Abu Huraira reported: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Hell complained to its Lord saying: O Lord, parts of me are consuming each other. So He allowed it two breaths: one in winter and one in summer."

meaning.en: The triliteral root Ḥ-Q-F (ح-ق-ف) refers to a curved sand dune or a winding tract of sand. In the Quran, it appears in the plural form al-Aḥqāf (الأحقاف), the name of Surah 46, which refers to the sand dunes region where the prophet Hūd was sent to the people of ʿĀd. The root evokes a desolate, wind-swept desert landscape.
meaning.ar: الْحَاءُ وَالْقَافُ وَالْفَاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى اسْتِطَالَةٍ فِي انْعِرَاجٍ

hadith.en: Ibn Abbas commented on the verse: 'Al-Ahqaf is mountains of sand in al-Shihr (a coastal region in Yemen).'

meaning.en: The quadriliteral root H-D-H-D (ه-د-ه-د) denotes the hoopoe bird (Upupa epops), a distinctive crested bird known in Arabic folklore. In the Quran, the hoopoe appears in the story of Prophet Solomon (Sulaymān), serving as a scout who brings news of the kingdom of Sheba and its queen Bilqīs. The bird is portrayed as intelligent, observant, and faithful in service.
meaning.ar: الْهَاءُ وَالدَّالُ وَالْهَاءُ وَالدَّالُ: الْهُدْهُدُ طَائِرٌ مَعْرُوفٌ

meaning.en: The triliteral root L-W-T (ل-و-ت) in the Quran is associated with the word لات (lāta), a rare negative particle meaning "not" or "not at all", appearing in the phrase وَلَاتَ حِينَ مَنَاصٍ ("but there was no time for escape") at 38:3. Classical grammarians differ on its derivation — some analyze it as a combination of لَا (negation) and تَ (an emphatic suffix), while others trace it to a root ل-و-ت with the sense of deficiency or cessation.
meaning.ar: لَاتَ مَعْنَاهَا لَيْسَ، وَهِيَ لَا زِيدَتْ فِيهَا التَّاءُ

meaning.en: The triliteral root M-J-S (م-ج-س) refers to the Magians (al-Majūs), commonly identified as Zoroastrians. In the Quran, they are listed in one verse (22:17) among the religious communities — alongside believers, Jews, Sabians, Christians, and polytheists — whom God will judge on the Day of Resurrection. The term was used in pre-Islamic Arabia and early Islam for the Persian Zoroastrian priestly class.
meaning.ar: الْمِيمُ وَالْجِيمُ وَالسِّينُ: الْمَجُوسُ جِنْسٌ مِنَ الْكُفَّارِ

hadith.en: The Prophet ﷺ said regarding the Magians: 'Treat them as you treat the People of the Book.' (Muwatta Malik — indicating Magians were given protected status.)

meaning.en: The quadriliteral root KH-R-Ṭ-M (خ-ر-ط-م) denotes the snout or trunk, particularly of an elephant or pig. In the Quran, it appears in Surah Al-Qalam (68:16) as a vivid metaphorical expression: ‘We will brand him upon the snout’ (سَنَسِمُهُ عَلَى الْخُرْطُومِ). This refers to a prominent disbeliever (al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīrah or similar) who will be disfigured or marked for disgrace on the Day of Judgment — the snout being the most prominent and sensitive part of the face.
meaning.ar: الْخَاءُ وَالرَّاءُ وَالطَّاءُ وَالْمِيمُ لَيْسَ بِأَصْلٍ، وَالْخُرْطُومُ: طَرَفُ الْأَنْفِ

hadith.en: Ibn Abbas said: 'This verse was revealed concerning al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīrah.' (Tafsir sources — referring to 68:16.)

shades.name_en: Metaphorical branding on the snout as divine punishment
shades.explanation: 'We will brand him upon the snout' — a powerful metaphor for public humiliation and divine marking of the guilty, using the animalistic term 'snout' to degrade the arrogant opponent.
